questions.question: A CDN receives 100,000 cacheable requests per second at a 92% hit rate. How many requests per second reach the origin path?
questions.explanation: Eight percent are misses, so 100,000 x 0.08 equals 8,000 origin-bound requests per second.

questions.question: What is the strongest cache-key rule?
options: Include only dimensions that change the authorized representation
Use a random key per request
questions.explanation: A key must separate genuinely different or differently authorized representations without fragmenting equivalent requests.

questions.question: Why use content-hashed URLs for static assets?
options: They make a changed object a new cache key, so old versions can remain immutable
They force every request to the origin
questions.explanation: A hash in the URL changes when bytes change, allowing long immutable caching without ambiguous invalidation.

questions.question: What does an origin shield primarily protect against?
options: Many edge misses fetching the same object independently
questions.explanation: A shield concentrates and coalesces misses so regional or global demand does not stampede the origin.

questions.question: When is stale-if-error an unsafe fallback?
options: For a personalized authorization decision whose old value may grant access
questions.explanation: Stale delivery must respect correctness and authorization boundaries; an old access decision can be unsafe.

questions.question: An edge region fails over successfully, but the origin still overloads. What likely changed?
options: The replacement route has cold caches and sends more misses downstream
The HTML gained a semantic heading
The origin no longer receives traffic
questions.explanation: Reachability failover can move traffic to cold caches, creating a miss surge that consumes shield and origin capacity.
